content.text: The response caching middleware is an HTTP cache living in your process: it stores what the response headers allow and serves it only when the request headers allow, so a client that sends
skips it. Output caching is the server-side cache you actually control: your policy decides what's stored and for how long, clients can't bypass it, and you can evict entries when data changes.

on every request, a setting someone added years ago to avoid stale screens, and the middleware obeys it. And when marketing edits the featured list, there's no way to clear what browsers and the CDN already keep.
The belief: adding the response caching middleware gives the server its own response cache. You register it, mark an endpoint, and the server stores the response and reuses it on your terms.

It's a reasonable belief. The name says "response caching", and the middleware really does store responses in server memory. Tests with curl or Postman show it working, because those tools send no caching headers unless you ask. The
attribute looks like server configuration. And before .NET 7 this was the only built-in way to cache whole responses, so years of tutorials present it as the server cache.
What's missing is who makes the rules. The middleware follows the HTTP caching standard, RFC 9111, and in that standard the client has a say.
Response caching is an HTTP cache inside your app

Your headers reach everyone else too

Output caching, added in .NET 7, works the other way around. A policy on the server decides which endpoints are cached, for how long (60 seconds by default), how the key varies, and which tags an entry carries. In the same test,

The fix: let the server own its cache

. Output caching skips authenticated requests by default, but only when
: in the wrong order, the test served a signed-in user the anonymous page.

blocks.title: Each server keeps its own copy

content.text: The default output cache store lives in process memory, so every instance behind a load balancer has its own entries, and they disappear on restart. An eviction only reaches the store it's called on. With several instances, use the Redis store (
) so evictions and entries are shared.
